steps.text: Part 2 of 5: Your first moves: three habits. This part covers The three habits. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

The **centre** is the four middle squares: d4, e4, d5 and e5. Knights and bishops see the most squares from the middle (the next board shows a knight with eight against two). [I] That is why pawns and minor pieces are drawn there early. A pawn there also takes squares from the enemy and opens paths for your bishops and queen. That gives habit one: **start with a centre pawn**.

steps.caption: The knight on d4 reaches eight squares, the one on the h-file four, and the one in the corner two.

steps.text: What do the strongest players choose? Our own database holds 329,379 games between players rated 2500 or higher [V]. White's first move was e4 in 43% of them, d4 in 36%, Nf3 in 12% and c4 in 8%. The first two are centre pawns. [I] The other two fight for the centre from a distance, a second way to follow the same habit.

steps.caption: The d-pawn also opens a path, this time for the bishop on c1 and the queen on d1.

line.say: The bishop steps outside its own pawns to an active square instead of staying boxed in.

steps.text: To **develop** a piece means to bring it off its starting row to a square where it works. Habit two: bring out your knights and bishops, and bring out a new piece each time instead of moving one piece again and again. Capablanca (*Chess Fundamentals*) and Emanuel Lasker (*Common Sense in Chess*) both urged quick development, usually knights before bishops [S: our source sheets]. Treat it as a default.

steps.caption: Four moves, four pieces out. Each piece has a job.

line.say: The knight comes out toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight too, and guards its pawn.
The bishop comes out and aims at the pawn on f7.
Black answers with the same idea and aims at f2.

steps.text: A **tempo** is one move of time. Count the moves, not just the pieces: if you spend two moves on one knight, your opponent has used the same two moves to bring out two pieces. Nimzowitsch (*My System*) treated development as teamwork, where the side ahead in it holds the initiative [S: our source sheet]. [I] Counting tempi is a rule of thumb, not a law: a second move is fine when it wins something or answers a threat. [H] Beginners notice lost tempi sooner when they count moves aloud.

steps.caption: Seven moves in. White has a knight, a bishop and a castled king working. Black has a pawn and one knight that went twice. Count the moves, not the pieces. [I] That gap is what players call losing time.

line.say: White opens with a centre pawn.
A knight comes out and attacks the pawn on e5.
Black develops a knight and guards the pawn.
The same knight moves again. Black has used two moves on it.
White castles. Three pieces are working, against one for Black.

steps.title: Same knight, other square
steps.prompt: Both Nf3 and Nh3 bring the knight out. Predict first: do they work equally well?

steps.text: **Remember.** The centre pawn comes first because it takes space and opens paths for your bishops and queen. Then bring out a new piece each move, because a tempo is one move of time and every extra move on one piece lets your opponent develop another. Ask yourself: which piece is not working yet? It fails when a move wins something or answers a threat.
